subject: biology

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a ligand and its receptor?
items.correct: The ligand binds reversibly to a binding site on the receptor protein that is complementary to it, and the receptor changes shape.
items.misconception: The receptor's binding site converts the ligand into a product, in the way an enzyme's active site converts a substrate.
items.why: Receptor binding is taught with the same lock-and-key or induced-fit language as enzymes, and 'binding site' sounds like 'active site'. Students transfer the whole enzyme model, including the chemical change of the substrate, to receptors. A receptor is not a catalyst for its ligand. The ligand binds and unbinds unchanged; what changes is the conformation of the receptor protein, which initiates a signal transduction pathway. (Some receptors are enzymes, such as tyrosine kinase receptors, but they act on themselves and on other proteins, not on the ligand.)
items.specStatementText: Receptors are proteins that bind one specific ligand
items.random_wrong: Any ligand reaching a cell binds to it, because every cell carries receptors for every signalling chemical in the body.

items.q: Epinephrine (adrenaline) released into the blood reaches every organ. Liver cells respond to it by breaking down glycogen, but some other cell types show no response at all. What best explains this difference?
items.correct: Only the liver cells have receptor proteins whose binding sites are complementary to epinephrine.
items.misconception: The blood carries epinephrine straight to the liver, so none reaches the other cell types.
items.why: Diagrams draw a single arrow from the gland to 'the target organ', and hormones are named by one effect, so students think the circulation routes the hormone to one place. Hormones have distant and often widespread effects because the blood carries them to every organ. Epinephrine, for example, acts on liver, muscle, heart and airway cells at once. Localized effects are characteristic of neurotransmitters at synapses, not of hormones.
items.specStatementText: Receptors are proteins that bind one specific ligand
items.random_wrong: Epinephrine can pass through the membrane of a liver cell but not through the membranes of the other cells.

items.q: Vibrio fischeri produces light when packed at high density inside the light organ of a squid, but not when living at low density in seawater. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Autoinducer secreted by each cell only reaches the threshold that switches on the light-producing genes when cells are dense.
items.misconception: The squid releases a chemical into its light organ that switches on the light-producing genes of the bacteria living there.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'sensing' suggests perceiving something outside, and the squid example makes the host the obvious candidate for the signal. Students also expect a 'count' of cells to require direct contact. In quorum sensing the signalling chemical is made and secreted by the bacteria themselves. Its concentration is a proxy for population density: only when enough cells are secreting does it reach the threshold at which it binds receptors and changes gene expression, so V. fischeri glows in the dense light-organ population but not when free-living in seawater.
items.specStatementText: Bacteria count themselves with a shared secreted signal
items.random_wrong: Each bacterium switches on its light-producing genes independently when its supply of nutrients in the light organ is high enough.

items.q: What is quorum sensing in bacteria?
items.correct: A change in gene expression across a population when a secreted signal reaches a threshold concentration.
items.misconception: Bacteria of one species each responding on their own to the concentration of nutrients in their environment.
items.why: Signalling is introduced through hormones and neurons in animals, and unicellular organisms are described as 'independent' cells. Students therefore assume bacterial behaviour is decided cell by cell. Bacteria signal to each other. In Vibrio fischeri each cell secretes an autoinducer, and bioluminescence is switched on only when the population is dense enough for the autoinducer to pass its threshold. Light production at low density would waste energy without producing useful light, so coordination through signalling is advantageous.
items.specStatementText: Bacteria count themselves with a shared secreted signal
items.random_wrong: Bacteria counting neighbouring cells through direct contact between the surface proteins of their cell walls.

items.q: Which statement about the functional categories of signalling chemicals in animals is correct?
items.correct: Cytokines are small proteins, secreted mainly by cells of the immune system, that act mostly on nearby cells.
items.misconception: Calcium ions are secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood and carried to distant target organs.
items.why: Students meet calcium mainly as a mineral in bones and diet and as a blood level that is regulated by hormones, so they picture it as a substance carried in blood rather than as an ion whose cytoplasmic concentration changes within a cell. Calcium ions are a distinct functional category: they are not made by the cell or secreted by a gland. Signalling depends on a sudden rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration when channels open, followed by pumps removing it again, and the effect is within the cell in which the change occurs.
items.specStatementText: Four functional categories of animal signalling chemicals
items.random_wrong: Cytokines are secreted by endocrine glands into the blood, from which they act on distant organs.

items.q: Noradrenaline is released by sympathetic neurons into synaptic gaps and is also released by the adrenal glands into the blood. What does this show about the categories hormone and neurotransmitter?
items.correct: They are functional categories, so one chemical can belong to either depending on how it is released and reaches its target.
items.misconception: Noradrenaline must be a hormone rather than a neurotransmitter, since a chemical belongs to only one category.
items.why: Hormones and the nervous system are taught in separate topics with separate example lists, and 'chemical messenger' categories are assumed to be chemical categories. Students rarely meet a substance that appears on both lists. The categories hormone, neurotransmitter, cytokine and calcium ion are functional. A hormone is transported in the blood to distant cells; a neurotransmitter diffuses across a synaptic gap to an adjacent cell. Noradrenaline does both, and chemically diverse substances (amines, peptides, amino acids, steroids) are found within the same functional category.
items.specStatementText: Four functional categories of animal signalling chemicals
items.random_wrong: In both cases the noradrenaline is carried in the blood to the cells it acts on, so the two categories cannot be distinguished.

items.q: To which chemical groups do the hormones epinephrine, insulin and testosterone belong?
items.correct: Epinephrine is an amine, insulin is a protein and testosterone is a steroid.
items.misconception: Epinephrine, insulin and testosterone are all proteins made of amino acids.
items.why: Insulin is the hormone example used throughout earlier courses and is described as a protein made by the pancreas; students generalise from the one example whose chemistry they know. The guide requires three chemical groups of hormones: amines (epinephrine), proteins (insulin) and steroids (oestradiol, progesterone, testosterone). Their different chemistry determines whether they act on transmembrane or intracellular receptors.
items.specStatementText: Signalling chemicals are chemically diverse, and that is useful
items.random_wrong: Epinephrine is a steroid, insulin is a protein and testosterone is a steroid as well.

items.q: Why is it advantageous for animals to use a wide range of chemically different substances as signalling chemicals rather than a single one?
items.correct: Many messages can travel in the same fluid at once, each read only by cells with the matching receptor.
items.misconception: The chemical nature of a signal does not matter, because a receptor recognises the message rather than the shape of the molecule.
items.why: Receptors are introduced as 'receiving a message', which suggests the message is separate from the molecule; students do not connect the specificity of the binding site to the chemistry of the ligand. Because receptor binding sites are specific to their ligand, a chemically distinct ligand for each message prevents cross-talk between the many signals present simultaneously. Chemistry also sets properties: hydrophobic steroids can reach intracellular receptors, small hydrophilic molecules act fast at surface receptors and are quickly removed.
items.specStatementText: Signalling chemicals are chemically diverse, and that is useful
items.random_wrong: Hormones must be large molecules and neurotransmitters small ones, so each category needs its own chemical class.

items.q: Chemical X is released from one cell, diffuses about 20 nm and acts on a single adjacent cell within a millisecond before being broken down. Chemical Y is released into the blood and, over several minutes, acts on cells in the liver, heart and skeletal muscle. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: X is a neurotransmitter acting locally across a synaptic gap, and Y is a hormone acting at a distance after transport in the blood.
items.misconception: Both are hormones, because a chemical released from a cell to act on another cell has to travel through the blood.
items.why: Both hormones and neurotransmitters are introduced as 'chemical messengers', and the blood is the only transport system students associate with chemical messages. Synapses are drawn without the scale that shows how tiny the gap is. Neurotransmitter action is localized: release from the presynaptic membrane, diffusion across a synaptic gap of about 20 nm, binding to the postsynaptic cell, then rapid removal. Hormones, by contrast, are transported by the blood system and act at a distance.
items.specStatementText: Hormones act far away; neurotransmitters act next door
items.random_wrong: Y is a neurotransmitter, because a hormone would be delivered by the blood to a single target organ rather than to several.

items.q: Insulin is a hydrophilic protein and oestradiol is a hydrophobic steroid. Where are their receptors, and do the hormones enter their target cells?
items.correct: Insulin stays outside and binds a transmembrane receptor; oestradiol passes through the membrane and binds an intracellular receptor.
items.misconception: Both stay outside and bind receptors on the cell surface, because all receptors are proteins embedded in the plasma membrane.
items.why: Every receptor drawn in earlier courses is a shape on the outside of a cell, and 'receptor' is linked with 'receiving' something from outside. Intracellular receptors are never pictured. Steroid hormones diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer and bind receptors inside the cell, in the cytoplasm or nucleus; the activated receptor then binds DNA. Transmembrane receptors serve ligands that cannot cross the membrane.
items.specStatementText: Surface receptors for ligands that stay out; internal receptors for ligands that get in
items.random_wrong: Both enter the cell, because a signalling chemical has to reach the cytoplasm in order to bring about any response at all.

items.q: The amino acid sequence of a newly discovered receptor shows seven stretches of about 20 mostly hydrophobic amino acids, separated by hydrophilic regions. Its ligand, a short peptide, binds to one of the hydrophilic regions. What can be concluded?
items.correct: It is a transmembrane receptor: the hydrophobic stretches span the bilayer and the ligand binds a hydrophilic part outside.
items.misconception: It is an intracellular receptor, because a protein containing hydrophilic regions could not remain embedded within the lipid bilayer.
items.why: Students learn that the membrane interior is hydrophobic and reason that anything in the membrane must be hydrophobic throughout, forgetting that the receptor also has to project into watery surroundings on both sides. Only the membrane-spanning region is hydrophobic. The parts exposed to the extracellular fluid and the cytoplasm are hydrophilic, which keeps the binding site accessible to a water-soluble ligand and the cytoplasmic domain able to interact with proteins inside the cell.
items.specStatementText: Surface receptors for ligands that stay out; internal receptors for ligands that get in
items.random_wrong: It is a transmembrane receptor whose ligand enters the cell through the hydrophilic regions to act in the cytoplasm.

items.q: What is meant by the initiation of a signal transduction pathway by a receptor?
items.correct: Ligand binding changes the receptor's shape, setting off a sequence of responses in the cell.
items.misconception: The ligand enters the cytoplasm after binding and itself performs the response inside the cell.
items.why: Statements such as 'adrenaline causes glycogen breakdown' compress a whole pathway into a single verb, so students picture the hormone as the agent performing the final step. Receptors initiate signal transduction pathways: binding of a ligand sets off a chain of events inside the cell, and it is the components of that chain, not the ligand, that produce the response. This is why one hormone can produce different responses in different cell types.
items.specStatementText: Receptor activation starts a chain of events inside the cell
items.random_wrong: The receptor converts the ligand into a product, and the product produced is the cell's response.

items.q: Acetylcholine released at a neuromuscular junction binds to acetylcholine receptors in the membrane of a muscle fibre. What happens next?
items.correct: An ion channel in the receptor opens, positive ions diffuse into the fibre and the membrane potential becomes less negative.
items.misconception: Acetylcholine passes through the channel in the receptor, carrying its positive charge into the fibre with it.
items.why: The neurotransmitter and the ions both 'go across' something in the same diagram, and the sentence 'binding opens a channel' is easily read as 'the channel is for the thing that binds'. The acetylcholine receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel: binding of acetylcholine on the extracellular face opens a channel through which positively charged ions diffuse into the cell. Acetylcholine stays outside and is later broken down in the synaptic gap by acetylcholinesterase.
items.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter receptors open channels and change the voltage
items.random_wrong: An ion channel in the receptor opens, positively charged ions leave the fibre and the inside becomes more negative.

items.q: A muscle fibre has a resting membrane potential of -70 mV. When acetylcholine is applied, the potential changes to -50 mV within 1 ms. If sodium ions are first removed from the fluid outside the fibre, acetylcholine still binds but the potential stays at -70 mV. What do these results show?
items.correct: The change to -50 mV is caused by Na+ diffusing into the fibre through channels opened by acetylcholine binding.
items.misconception: The change to -50 mV is caused by positive ions leaving the fibre, a movement that needs sodium outside to draw them out.
items.why: The resting potential is a negative number (about -70 mV) and students struggle with the sign convention, so 'a change in voltage' is as likely to be imagined as more negative as less negative. Diagrams of pumps moving Na+ out are also remembered. Na+ is at high concentration outside the cell, so when the receptor channel opens Na+ diffuses inward down its concentration gradient. Inflow of positive charge makes the inside less negative; this is depolarization, and it may cause other changes such as an action potential.
items.specStatementText: Neurotransmitter receptors open channels and change the voltage
items.random_wrong: Acetylcholine itself enters through the channel, but it can only do so if it is carried in by sodium ions.

items.q: How does a G protein-coupled receptor convey a signal into a cell?
items.correct: Binding of the ligand outside changes the receptor's shape, activating a G protein on the inner face, which then activates an effector.
items.misconception: The ligand passes through a channel in the receptor and binds directly to the G protein, which lies in the cytoplasm just beneath the membrane.
items.why: The name 'G protein-coupled receptor' is read as 'receptor made of G protein', and the acetylcholine receptor example, which is a channel, is generalised to every transmembrane receptor. A GPCR conveys the signal across the membrane by a conformational change: ligand binding outside alters the cytoplasmic part of the receptor, which activates a G protein bound to the inner face of the membrane. The activated G protein then switches on an effector such as adenylyl cyclase. Nothing passes through the receptor.
items.specStatementText: Some receptors pass the signal to a G protein
items.random_wrong: The G protein is released from the membrane into the blood as a second messenger that carries the signal to neighbouring cells of the tissue.

items.q: A hormone binds to a G protein-coupled receptor on cells, and an enzyme inside the cells becomes active. A toxin that locks the G protein in its inactive form is added. The hormone still binds to the receptor, but the enzyme is no longer activated. What does this show?
items.correct: The G protein is needed to convey the signal from the occupied receptor to the enzyme inside.
items.misconception: The G protein converts the bound hormone into cAMP, so without it no second messenger can be formed.
items.why: Pathway summaries list 'receptor, G protein, cAMP' and students collapse the sequence, giving the G protein the job of the enzyme that lies between it and cAMP. The G protein's role is to convey the signal from the receptor to an effector. In the epinephrine pathway the effector is adenylyl cyclase, and the second messenger cAMP it produces activates kinases that switch on glycogen breakdown.
items.specStatementText: Some receptors pass the signal to a G protein
items.random_wrong: The toxin has blocked the channel in the receptor through which the hormone normally enters the cell.

items.q: Which sequence correctly describes the events after epinephrine (adrenaline) binds to its receptor on a liver cell?
items.correct: A G protein is activated, adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP, and cAMP activates kinases that switch on glycogen breakdown.
items.misconception: Epinephrine enters the liver cell and directly activates the enzymes that break down glycogen into glucose.
items.why: Phrases such as 'insulin lets glucose into cells' and 'adrenaline makes the liver release glucose' suggest the hormone goes in and does the job. Steroid hormones, which do enter, are then generalised to all hormones. Whether the signalling chemical penetrates the cell depends on its chemistry. Hydrophilic hormones (proteins, peptides, amines) remain outside and act on transmembrane receptors; only hydrophobic ligands such as steroids pass through the membrane to intracellular receptors.
items.specStatementText: Epinephrine acts through a G protein and cAMP
items.random_wrong: cAMP is released from the liver cell into the blood as a second messenger that acts on other liver cells.

items.q: Binding of a few molecules of epinephrine to receptors on a liver cell leads to the release of many thousands of glucose molecules. Which feature of the signalling pathway explains this?
items.correct: Each activated G protein, adenylyl cyclase and kinase acts on many molecules of the next component, amplifying the signal.
items.misconception: The pathway cannot amplify the signal, so the cell must in fact have bound many thousands of epinephrine molecules at the same time.
items.why: Students reason stoichiometrically, as in chemical equations, and diagrams of pathways draw one molecule at each step, hiding the fact that each activated enzyme turns over many substrate molecules. Signal transduction cascades amplify: a single activated receptor can activate several G proteins, each activated adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP molecules, and each activated kinase phosphorylates many enzyme molecules. A few hormone molecules in the blood can therefore release a great deal of glucose from a liver cell.
items.specStatementText: Epinephrine acts through a G protein and cAMP
items.random_wrong: The receptor converts each epinephrine molecule it binds into an active enzyme, and that enzyme releases the glucose.

items.q: Which sequence correctly describes how insulin increases glucose uptake by a muscle cell?
items.correct: Insulin binds the receptor outside; tyrosines on its cytoplasmic part are phosphorylated; a cascade moves vesicles with glucose transporters to the membrane.
items.misconception: Insulin enters the cell bound to glucose and releases it in the cytoplasm; the empty insulin then returns to the blood to collect more glucose.
items.why: The GCSE summary 'insulin causes glucose to move into cells' names no mechanism, so students imagine insulin as a carrier that takes glucose in with it. Insulin is a protein and cannot cross the membrane. Its receptor has tyrosine kinase activity: binding causes phosphorylation of tyrosine inside the cell, which starts a sequence of reactions ending with more glucose transporters in the plasma membrane. Glucose then enters through those transporters by facilitated diffusion.
items.specStatementText: Insulin's receptor phosphorylates itself, and glucose transporters arrive
items.random_wrong: Insulin binds the receptor, which phosphorylates free tyrosine in the cytoplasm; the phosphorylated tyrosine then binds glucose molecules and pulls them into the cell.

items.q: How does a steroid hormone such as testosterone change the expression of genes in a target cell?
items.correct: It enters the cell and activates a receptor inside it, which binds specific DNA sequences to promote transcription.
items.misconception: It diffuses through the membrane into the nucleus and binds directly to the DNA at the start of the genes it switches on.
items.why: Statements such as 'testosterone switches on genes' omit the receptor, and the hormone is the only molecule named, so students give it the DNA-binding role. A steroid hormone has no DNA-binding ability. Its intracellular receptor, once activated by ligand binding, binds specific DNA sequences and promotes transcription of particular genes; it is the receptor protein that recognises the DNA.
items.specStatementText: Steroid hormones enter the cell and switch on genes
items.random_wrong: It binds a receptor in the plasma membrane, and this receptor then detaches and travels to the nucleus to bind the DNA.

items.q: Cells respond to testosterone only after about 30 minutes, and the response is abolished by a drug that blocks transcription. The same cells respond to epinephrine within seconds, and this response is unaffected by the drug. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: Testosterone acts via an intracellular receptor that promotes transcription, so its effect needs new mRNA; epinephrine acts on enzymes already present.
items.misconception: Testosterone is slow because it must be carried across the membrane by a transport protein, and the drug blocks that carrier.
items.why: Earlier courses describe membranes as barriers that let water and small solutes through, and 'hydrophobic' is heard as 'repelled', so students assume a hydrophobic molecule is kept out. The centre of the bilayer is hydrophobic, so it is hydrophilic molecules that are excluded and need transmembrane receptors or transport proteins. Hydrophobic ligands penetrate the cell and bind intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
items.specStatementText: Steroid hormones enter the cell and switch on genes
items.random_wrong: The drug prevents testosterone itself from binding to the DNA of the target genes, which is why the response to testosterone is lost.

items.q: For most of the menstrual cycle, oestradiol reduces the secretion of GnRH by cells in the hypothalamus. Late in the follicular phase, when oestradiol has been at a high level for about two days, GnRH secretion increases sharply. What best explains these observations?
items.correct: Oestradiol's effect on GnRH-secreting cells switches from inhibition at moderate levels to stimulation at high sustained levels.
items.misconception: Oestradiol can only inhibit GnRH secretion, so the sharp increase must have been caused by a different hormone.
items.why: Negative feedback is taught first and is the general rule in homeostasis, so students treat oestradiol's inhibition of GnRH as its only possible effect on those cells. The effect of oestradiol on GnRH-secreting cells depends on its concentration and duration: low to moderate levels inhibit, high sustained levels stimulate. The switch to positive feedback is what drives ovulation.
items.specStatementText: What oestradiol does in the hypothalamus and progesterone in the endometrium
items.random_wrong: The early reduction was a harmful side effect of oestradiol and the later increase is its beneficial action.

items.q: What is the effect of progesterone on the cells of the endometrium?
items.correct: It maintains and thickens the endometrium, making its glands secrete and increasing its blood supply for implantation.
items.misconception: It causes the endometrium to break down and be shed, which is why menstruation happens while progesterone is being secreted.
items.why: Menstruation is the most memorable event of the cycle and hormones are known to control it, so students attach the shedding to the hormone rather than to its withdrawal. Progesterone acts on endometrial cells to maintain the lining; it is the fall in progesterone at the end of the cycle that removes this support and leads to menstruation.
items.specStatementText: What oestradiol does in the hypothalamus and progesterone in the endometrium
items.random_wrong: It binds directly to the DNA of the endometrial cells and switches on the genes that cause growth of the lining.

items.q: What is the difference between negative feedback and positive feedback in the regulation of signalling pathways?
items.correct: In negative feedback the response reduces the stimulus; in positive feedback the response increases it.
items.misconception: Negative feedback produces harmful effects in the body, whereas positive feedback produces beneficial effects.
items.why: In everyday use 'negative' and 'positive' are judgements of value, as in feedback on a piece of work, and students carry that meaning into biology. In cell signalling, negative feedback (such as oestradiol inhibiting GnRH secretion) keeps a variable near a set level, and positive feedback (such as oxytocin during birth) drives a process to completion. Neither term implies good or bad.
items.specStatementText: Negative feedback opposes change; positive feedback amplifies it
items.random_wrong: Negative feedback lowers the level of a variable, whereas positive feedback raises the level of a variable.

items.q: During birth, stretching of the cervix stimulates secretion of oxytocin, which strengthens contractions of the uterus, which stretch the cervix further, until the baby is delivered. How should this regulation be described?
items.correct: Positive feedback, because each response increases the stimulus that caused it until an end point is reached.
items.misconception: Negative feedback, because the whole process is switched off once the baby has been delivered.
items.why: Students map 'negative' onto 'decrease' and 'positive' onto 'increase', helped by examples in which the corrected variable happens to be too high, such as blood glucose after a meal. The defining feature is the relationship between response and stimulus: in negative feedback the response reduces the stimulus, in positive feedback the response increases it. A process that eventually stops, such as birth, can still be driven by positive feedback.
items.specStatementText: Negative feedback opposes change; positive feedback amplifies it
items.random_wrong: Negative feedback, because the outcome of the process is beneficial to both the mother and the baby.

items.q: A hormone in the blood reaches every cell in the body. Why do only some cells respond to it?
items.correct: Only cells that possess receptor proteins with a binding site complementary to that hormone respond; other cells are exposed to the hormone but have no receptor for it.
items.misconception: Any cell that a signalling chemical reaches will respond to it, so a hormone acts wherever the blood carries it.
items.why: Earlier courses describe hormones as being 'carried to the target organ', which suggests the chemical is delivered only where it acts and that arrival is what causes the response. Students do not meet the idea that the receptor, not the arrival of the chemical, decides whether a cell responds. Receptors are proteins with binding sites for specific signalling chemicals (ligands). The blood distributes a hormone throughout the body, but a cell responds only if it has receptors for that ligand; this specificity is what makes the effect targeted.
items.specStatementText: Receptors are proteins that bind one specific ligand
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do cytokines differ from hormones?
items.correct: Cytokines are small proteins secreted by many cell types, especially immune cells, and act mostly on nearby cells; hormones are secreted by endocrine cells and glands into the blood and act on distant cells.
items.misconception: Cytokines are simply the hormones of the immune system, made in glands and carried in the blood to distant organs.
items.why: Every animal signalling chemical met before IB is a hormone, so students file any new 'chemical messenger' as a hormone. The word 'cytokine' gives no clue about its local action. Cytokines form a separate functional category: their sources are ordinary cells rather than endocrine glands and their action is mainly local, coordinating cells in the immune response. Hormones are defined by transport in the blood to distant targets.
items.specStatementText: Four functional categories of animal signalling chemicals
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What kind of molecule is a steroid hormone such as testosterone?
items.correct: A lipid synthesized from cholesterol, with a four-ring carbon skeleton; it is hydrophobic and can pass through the phospholipid bilayer.
items.misconception: Steroids are proteins, because 'anabolic steroids' build muscle and muscle is protein.
items.why: The everyday association of steroids with muscle growth leads students to assume a steroid is itself a muscle-building protein. Steroids are lipids derived from cholesterol, not proteins. Their hydrophobic nature is why they cross the plasma membrane and bind intracellular receptors, unlike protein and amine hormones.
items.specStatementText: Signalling chemicals are chemically diverse, and that is useful
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all transmembrane receptors convey their signal in the same way?
items.correct: No. Ligand-gated ion channels such as the acetylcholine receptor change membrane potential directly, tyrosine kinase receptors phosphorylate proteins, and only G protein-coupled receptors act via a G protein; there are many hundreds of GPCRs alone.
items.misconception: Every transmembrane receptor works the same way, by activating a G protein and producing cAMP.
items.why: The syllabus presents three worked examples, and the G protein and cAMP pathway is the one most students remember, so they generalise it to every receptor. The guide requires students to appreciate that there are many G protein-coupled receptors in humans; they respond to hormones, neurotransmitters, odours and light, and are the targets of a large fraction of medicinal drugs. Ligand-gated channels alter membrane potential directly, tyrosine kinase receptors phosphorylate proteins, and intracellular receptors act on DNA.
items.specStatementText: Some receptors pass the signal to a G protein
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is a second messenger?
items.correct: A small molecule such as cAMP, produced inside the cell when a receptor is activated, that carries the message of the hormone (the first messenger, which stayed outside) to targets in the cytoplasm.
items.misconception: The second messenger is a second hormone, released by the target cell into the blood to pass the message on to other cells.
items.why: The only 'messengers' met earlier are hormones, so 'second messenger' is read as 'another hormone'. Pathways in which one gland's hormone stimulates another gland reinforce the idea. cAMP is made inside the cell from ATP by adenylyl cyclase when the G protein activated by the epinephrine receptor switches the enzyme on. It diffuses within the cytoplasm and activates protein kinases; it is not secreted and does not leave the cell.
items.specStatementText: Epinephrine acts through a G protein and cAMP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: To which chemical group does epinephrine (adrenaline) belong?
items.correct: It is an amine, a small molecule derived from the amino acid tyrosine.
items.misconception: Epinephrine is a steroid hormone, because it is produced by the adrenal gland like cortisol.
items.why: Adrenal cortex hormones such as cortisol are steroids, the word 'adrenal' appears in 'adrenaline', and both hormones are associated with stress, so students place them in the same chemical group. Epinephrine is a hydrophilic amine that binds transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors and acts through cAMP. Steroids are hydrophobic lipids from cholesterol that bind intracellular receptors; the two groups differ in chemistry, receptor location and mechanism.
items.specStatementText: Signalling chemicals are chemically diverse, and that is useful
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is phosphorylated when insulin binds its receptor?
items.correct: Tyrosine residues within the cytoplasmic part of the receptor protein itself (and subsequently tyrosines in other proteins), using phosphate from ATP.
items.misconception: The receptor phosphorylates free tyrosine amino acids floating in the cytoplasm, and these then act as the signal.
items.why: The syllabus phrase 'phosphorylation of tyrosine' names the amino acid without saying it is part of a protein, so students picture the free monomer. Tyrosine kinase receptors add phosphate groups to tyrosine residues that are built into polypeptides, first their own cytoplasmic domain and then downstream proteins. The phosphorylated proteins change shape and activity, which is how the sequence of reactions is propagated.
items.specStatementText: Insulin's receptor phosphorylates itself, and glucose transporters arrive
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do the extra glucose transporters in the membrane come from after insulin binds?
items.correct: From pre-formed transporters already stored in the membranes of vesicles in the cytoplasm; the vesicles move to and fuse with the plasma membrane within minutes.
items.misconception: The insulin signal switches on transcription of the transporter genes, and new glucose transporter proteins are synthesized and inserted in the membrane.
items.why: Students who have learned that steroid hormones work by switching on genes assume that any change in the amount of a protein in a cell requires new gene expression. The guide specifies movement of vesicles containing glucose transporters to the plasma membrane. Because the transporters already exist, the response is fast; recruiting stored proteins by vesicle fusion is a different mechanism from changing gene expression.
items.specStatementText: Insulin's receptor phosphorylates itself, and glucose transporters arrive
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How quickly do steroid hormones produce their effects compared with epinephrine?
items.correct: More slowly: steroid effects require transcription and translation of new proteins and take minutes to hours, whereas epinephrine alters the activity of existing enzymes within seconds.
items.misconception: Steroid hormones act as quickly as other hormones, because they enter the cell directly rather than having to signal through the membrane.
items.why: Entering the cell sounds more direct than a transduction pathway, so students expect it to be faster. The time needed to make mRNA and protein is not considered. Intracellular receptors affect gene expression, so the response is the appearance of new proteins, which takes time but is long-lasting. Transmembrane receptors acting via second messengers modify enzymes that already exist, giving fast responses.
items.specStatementText: Steroid hormones enter the cell and switch on genes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is positive feedback part of normal, healthy regulation?
items.correct: Yes. Positive feedback is used to drive a process rapidly to an end point, as when oxytocin strengthens contractions during birth or oestradiol triggers the LH surge; the loop ends when the end point is reached.
items.misconception: Positive feedback does not occur in healthy regulation; it is a runaway fault that only happens in disease.
items.why: Homeostasis is taught almost entirely through negative feedback, and 'vicious circle' examples such as fever or shock are the only positive feedback most students meet. Positive feedback is a normal regulatory mechanism for processes that must go to completion once started. It is self-limiting because the process removes the stimulus at its end point (delivery of the baby, ovulation).
items.specStatementText: Negative feedback opposes change; positive feedback amplifies it
